passage: I'm Sabina, and three interviews had ended with the same polite line about my missing experience. Then Bhupen read my portfolio and said, "Start on the fifteenth." I have never forgotten that. So when I found that the pricing sheet Bhupen had sent to two clients used the old tax rate, my chest went tight. It felt ungrateful to point at a mistake made by the person who took a chance on me. I waited a day. Then I walked over with the sheet in hand and said, "I think this rate is outdated. Could we check?" Bhupen looked, groaned, and said, "Thank you. Send me the corrected version and I will call both clients." I understood then that being honest was one of the ways of saying thanks.

qa.q: What was wrong with the pricing sheet Bhupen sent to two clients?
qa.a: It used the old tax rate.

qa.q: Why did Sabina wait a day before speaking up?
qa.a: Sabina felt it would be ungrateful to point at a mistake made by the person who had taken a chance on Sabina.

qa.q: What made Sabina's way of raising the error work well?
qa.a: Sabina brought the sheet and asked whether the rate could be checked, so Bhupen could fix it quickly without feeling blamed.

qa.q: How did Bhupen react to the correction?
qa.a: Bhupen thanked Sabina and planned to call both clients, which shows candid input was welcome.

grounding: The narrator, grateful to a manager who gave a chance, still points out an error, showing thanks and honesty can go together.

passage:
Nikita, beta, you're afraid to tell your boss she made an error because she gave you your first break. I understand. Let your Parul aunty tell you something.

When I was twenty-five, nobody wanted to hire a woman accountant who'd taken three years off for her father's illness. Mrs. D'Costa did. She said, "I trust you," and she meant it. I would have walked into fire for her.

Six months later, preparing the annual accounts, I found she had booked a large payment in the wrong year. It made the profit look better than it was. I was sick with worry. Who was I to correct her?

The turning point came when I remembered why she'd hired me. "I need someone who will tell me the truth," she'd said in the interview.

So I told her, quietly, with the papers. She read them, took off her glasses and said, "Thank you. That's exactly your job." She fixed it that day. And she trusted me more after.

qa.q: How many years had Parul taken off for her father's illness?
qa.a: She had taken three years off.

qa.q: How did young Parul feel when she found the wrong entry?
qa.a: She felt grateful to Mrs. D'Costa yet sick with worry about correcting her.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Parul's story?
qa.a: Remembering that Mrs. D'Costa hired her to tell the truth, she raised the error quietly with the papers.

qa.q: How did Mrs. D'Costa see Parul's correction?
qa.a: Mrs. D'Costa valued it, thanking her and saying it was exactly her job, and trusted her more afterwards.

grounding: An elder's story shows a young woman grateful to a manager who gave her a chance, who stays honest and points out the manager's error, and is valued for it.

passage:
The board presentation was in fifty minutes, the projector in the conference room had just died, and Gurpreet, rechecking the slides on a laptop, saw it: in Nirmala ma'am's summary, the growth figure was eighteen percent. The data said eight.

Gurpreet's stomach dropped. Nirmala had hired Gurpreet when three other managers had said no: "not enough experience". Everything since had come from that one chance. And now, fifty minutes before the board, Gurpreet had to say she was wrong?

The clock ticked. The IT man was still fiddling with the cables.

Gurpreet walked over and spoke quietly. "Ma'am, I think slide four has a typo. The data says eight percent, not eighteen. I'm so grateful for everything you've done for me, and that's why I had to say it."

Nirmala looked, went pale, then laughed shakily. "Eighteen would have been a disaster. Fix it, quickly."

After the meeting she said, "That's why I hired you."

qa.q: What growth figure did the data actually show?
What was Gurpreet feeling on seeing the error?
qa.a: Gurpreet's stomach dropped; Gurpreet felt grateful to Nirmala and afraid to correct her so close to the meeting.

qa.q: Why was speaking up the best way for Gurpreet to show gratitude?
qa.a: Honest input protected Nirmala from a disaster in front of the board, which served her better than silence.

qa.q: How did Nirmala respond to Gurpreet's correction?
qa.a: Nirmala was shaken, then relieved and appreciative, saying that was why she had hired Gurpreet.

grounding: The story shows a young employee grateful to a manager who took a chance on them, who stays honest and points out an error, and whose candour is valued.
